newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia reshuffles military high command.
newsitem.headline: Colombia reshuffles military high command.

text.p: The Colombian government announced a shakeup in the military high command on Thursday, two months after leftist rebels unleashed one of the bloodiest offensives in the country's long-running guerrilla war.

Defence Minister Juan Carlos Esguerra told a news conference armed forces commander Adm. Holdan Delgado was stepping down voluntarily from active service and had been replaced by Army chief Gen. Harold Bedoya.

Delgado, the first Navy man ever named military commander, was appointed just last year after his predecessor, Gen. Hernando Camilo Zuniga Chaparro, stepped down amid reports that his U.S. visa had been revoked because of his alleged ties to Cali cartel drug lords.

Bedoya, 57, who took over as army chief in 1994, is a veteran guerrilla fighter believed to be well connected with military officials in the United States, where he served as military attache at the Colombian embassy in 1985.

He also taught classes at the U.S. Army School of the Americas in Panama in 1979. Human rights groups allege he was also linked at that time to a right-wing paramilitary group in Bogota known as the American Anti-Communist Alliance or "Triple A."
As army chief, Bedoya has led a vocal campaign against leftist rebels, branding them "narco-guerrillas."
He accuses the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), the largest rebel group, of having become Colombia's leading drug trafficking organisation.
In remarks to reporters, Bedoya stressed what he termed the importance of reestablishing the "fuero militar," a controversial law that exempts armed forces members from trial by civilian courts.

Bedoya, who says the military needs more men and equipment to wage an effective counterinsurgency campaign, also said he hoped the cash-strapped government would do everything possible to help make it more efficient.

The army was humiliated when FARC rebels overran a southwestern military base in August. The raid, in which 30 soldiers were killed and 60 taken prisoner, marked the start of a nationwide offensive that army officials describe as one of the worst in more than three decades of conflict.

In addition to Bedoya's promotion, the Defence Ministry announced that the government had named new air force, army and navy commanders, as well as a new commander of the joint chiefs of staff, a largely ceremonial post in Colombia.
International watchdogs have alleged that the new army commander, Brig. Gen. Jose Manuel Bonett, has a history of human rights abuse.

A 1992 study called "State Terrorism in Colombia," compiled by Pax Christi International and other rights groups, linked Bonett to cases of torture and murder in 1990 in southwestern Valle del Cauca province, where he was head of the 3rd Army Brigade.

Amnesty International this week urged the United States to suspend arms sales and anti-drug aid to Colombia because of reports that Colombian army units involved in atrocities were using U.S.-supplied equipment.
